query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior under service-simulated conditions emerges because cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperatures induces localized nanoscale short-range ordering (or subtle compositional fluctuations) along grain boundaries and regions of high dislocation density. These localized zones act as stress concentrators that hinder plastic deformation and promote premature crack initiation, a mechanism distinct from the grain-boundary segregation and precipitate formation observed in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure and no pre-existing local chemical order.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperatures representative of demanding service conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments are conducted under service-relevant conditions combining high temperature and significant cyclic loading to activate atomic diffusion and mechanical strain.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of localized nanoscale regions of short-range chemical order (or subtle compositional fluctuations) at grain boundaries and dislocation intersections.
generation.mechanism: Under elevated temperature cyclic loading, enhanced atomic mobility promotes local elemental redistribution. This leads to the nucleation of small chemically ordered clusters or fluctuations that impede dislocation motion, thereby localizing stress and lowering the energy barrier for crack initiation, which results in a reduction of overall toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-processed homogeneous alloy, treated samples are expected to exhibit detectable nanoscale chemical ordering at stress concentration sites along grain boundaries and dislocation intersections, along with a measurable reduction in fracture toughness and a shift toward brittle, intergranular fracture behavior. This behavior contrasts with conventional alloys that typically embrittle via grain-boundary segregation with distinct precipitate formation.
generation.baseline: The as-processed, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous, disordered microstructure and high toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated under service conditions where high temperature and cyclic mechanical loading provide sufficient activation for local chemical redistribution; under lower temperatures or static loading, the effect may be negligible.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative relation between induced local order and toughness reduction is supported, the precise magnitude of toughness degradation and the critical loading/temperature thresholds require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two cohorts of high-entropy alloy specimens. One cohort is subjected to prolonged cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperatures representative of service conditions, while the other is maintained as the baseline under minimal loading and lower temperature. Use in situ high-resolution microscopy techniques (TEM, atom probe tomography) to monitor the development of nanoscale chemical ordering along grain boundaries and dislocation intersections and perform periodic mechanical toughness tests.
measurements: High-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography to detect and quantify nanoscale short-range ordering or compositional fluctuations at grain boundaries
Fracture toughness (K_IC) and ductility measurements from mechanical testing
Correlation analysis of localized ordering and crack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cyclically loaded high-temperature samples do not develop measurable nanoscale short-range ordering or compositional fluctuations, and if there is no statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness relative to the baseline specimens, the proposed mechanism is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, exposure to elevated service temperatures combined with cyclic mechanical loading induces local short-range chemical ordering, particularly along grain boundaries and high‐dislocation-density regions. This stress-assisted short-range ordering (SSRO) creates nanoscale domains of compositionally enriched, brittle phases that hinder dislocation motion and localize strain, leading to a degradation of toughness—a mechanism distinct from the classical grain‐boundary segregation observed in conventional alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure.
drafts.intervention: Subject samples to prolonged cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperatures representative of demanding service conditions.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature service environment (e.g., elevated temperatures around a critical threshold) combined with cyclic or dynamic loading conditions; comparison made with samples held at ambient temperature (or lower load conditions) to serve as a baseline.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale regions of short-range ordering (SSRO) that form along grain boundaries and dislocation intersections.
drafts.mechanism: Under high-temperature cyclic loading, thermal fluctuations and mechanical stress promote local compositional fluctuations that trigger the nucleation of chemically ordered clusters. These clusters, due to their distinct composition and structure, are intrinsically brittle and impede the normal dislocation-mediated plastic deformation, thus localizing stress and leading to premature fracture.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Samples under high-temperature cyclic loading will display the emergence of localized SSRO regions at grain boundaries, measurable via TEM or atom probe tomography, and a corresponding significant reduction in toughness compared to baseline samples maintained at low temperature or low load. In contrast, conventional alloys will show toughness loss primarily via grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation.
drafts.baseline: Single-phase high-entropy alloy samples maintained at lower temperatures with minimal cyclic loading, which should retain a homogeneous microstructure and high toughness.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected under service conditions involving elevated temperatures and cyclic loading; under static, low-temperature conditions the SSRO and associated toughness degradation should not occur, and other embrittlement mechanisms typical of conventional alloys remain absent.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two cohorts of identical single-phase high-entropy alloy samples. One cohort undergoes prolonged cyclic loading at an elevated temperature near the anticipated service condition limit, while the control cohort is kept at ambient temperature with minimal loading. Both groups are then subjected to fracture toughness testing. Microstructural analysis using TEM and atom probe tomography (APT) will be conducted to detect the presence of localized short-range ordering, particularly near grain boundaries.
measurements: Fracture toughness (K_IC) and ductility assessments (e.g., elongation to failure) for both cohorts
High-resolution TEM imaging and APT to identify and quantify nanoscale SSRO domains at grain boundaries
Comparative analysis of dislocation density and strain localization patterns using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-temperature cyclic loading samples do not develop any detectable SSRO regions or do not show a statistically significant reduction in toughness relative to the control group, then the hypothesis that SSRO acts as a mediator for brittleness is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy (HEA), brittle behavior emerges through stress-induced, nanoscale compositional fluctuations that lead to localized grain-boundary phase separation and the nucleation of ultrafine intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates reduce intergranular cohesion and promote brittle fracture under demanding service conditions.
drafts.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy without pre-existing grain-boundary second phases.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to cyclic mechanical loading combined with thermal exposure aimed at activating diffusion and stress effects.
drafts.conditions: Elevated temperatures near the alloy’s operational limits with cyclic or prolonged loading that mimic service conditions in demanding engineering applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates that form along grain boundaries due to local compositional segregation.
drafts.mechanism: Under thermal and mechanical stress, localized compositional fluctuations overcome the metastability of the single-phase state despite the high configurational entropy. This leads to the nucleation and growth of fine intermetallic phases along grain boundaries that act as preferential sites for crack initiation, ultimately degrading toughness.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous phase, the HEA will display increased brittle fracture behavior and reduced toughness, with TEM/EDS analysis revealing nanoscale grain-boundary precipitates that correlate with these mechanical property degradations.
drafts.baseline: The as-processed single-phase high-entropy alloy exhibiting a favorable combination of high toughness and ductility.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature and cyclic loading service conditions. Under lower temperature or static loading conditions, the diffusion and stress-driven segregation may not be sufficient to trigger precipitate formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a comparative study on samples of the HEA and a conventional alloy. Subject both to identical thermal-cycling and mechanical loading conditions. Use high-resolution TEM and EDS to monitor grain-boundary structures and perform fracture toughness tests at regular intervals during the experiment.
measurements: Grain-boundary precipitate size and density via TEM/EDS
Fracture toughness and ductility via mechanical testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA under the tested service conditions shows no significant formation of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries and retains its initial toughness and ductility—comparable to or better than the conventional alloy—then the hypothesis that stress-induced grain-boundary phase separation drives embrittlement is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are initially single‐phase, emergent brittle behavior under service-like conditions is driven by localized compositional fluctuations at grain boundaries. Even though classical grain-boundary precipitates are suppressed, subtle local deviations in solute distribution induce lattice distortions that lower the barrier for crack initiation and propagation along the grain boundaries.
drafts.material_initial_state: A single-phase high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous global composition and fine equiaxed grain structure.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal cycling and cooling treatments designed to gradually enhance local compositional fluctuations without triggering classical intermetallic precipitation or gross second-phase formation.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature service conditions combined with mechanical loading near yield levels, conditions under which even marginal reductions in toughness can be critical.
drafts.structural_mediator: Localized lattice distortions at grain boundaries arising from subtle compositional fluctuations.
drafts.mechanism: During thermal cycling, even in a single-phase HEA, slight local modulations in solute concentration develop at grain boundaries. These fluctuations create regionally distinct lattice strain fields, which impede efficient dislocation nucleation and motion. Under load, these strained regions act as stress concentrators that favor intergranular crack initiation and propagation, leading to brittle failure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Samples that undergo thermal treatments promoting local compositional fluctuations will show a lower fracture toughness and a more intergranular fracture mode compared to the baseline untouched alloy, which maintains high strength–ductility. This trend contrasts with conventional alloys where grain-boundary precipitation is the main culprit for brittleness.
drafts.baseline: The initial single-phase HEA with a homogeneous composition and minimal local compositional fluctuations exhibits balanced strength and ductility with no indication of intergranular embrittlement.
drafts.boundary: This mechanistic effect is expected to become significant under service conditions that combine high temperature (or thermal cycling) with mechanical loads approaching the yield strength. Under milder conditions, the induced fluctuations may not be sufficient to trigger brittleness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA samples subjected to varying levels of controlled thermal cycling and cooling rates to induce differing degrees of local compositional fluctuations. Assess mechanical properties via tensile testing and fracture toughness measurements while concurrently characterizing grain-boundary chemistry and lattice distortions using techniques such as TEM, EDS, and EBSD.
measurements: High-resolution TEM/EDS analysis of grain-boundary chemistry and local compositional fluctuations
EBSD mapping for assessing grain-boundary misorientation and associated strain fields
Fracture surface examination to distinguish intergranular from transgranular crack propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the degree of induced local compositional fluctuations (as verified by microscopy and chemical analysis) does not correlate with a measurable reduction in fracture toughness or a shift toward intergranular fracture modes, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior emerges not from classic grain-boundary segregation and precipitate formation but from a stress-induced, nanoscale redistribution of constituent elements that leads to the formation of short-range ordered regions along intense deformation zones (e.g., dislocation pile-ups). These locally ordered nanodomains cause premature crack initiation despite the alloy’s overall compositionally homogeneous state.
drafts.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy that has been processed to suppress rapid grain coarsening and intermetallic phase formation.
drafts.intervention: Subject the HEA to controlled cyclic mechanical loading (or high strain-rate deformation) under service-simulated conditions, while monitoring in situ the local microstructural evolution.
drafts.conditions: Tests would be performed at service-relevant temperatures and strain rates where significant plastic deformation occurs, contrasting regions of high local plastic strain with minimally deformed regions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The intervention is expected to induce the formation of localized short-range order (SRO) or compositional heterogeneity in the vicinity of dislocation structures or slip bands.
drafts.mechanism: Under high plastic strain, the inherent chemical complexity leads to local differential diffusion or redistribution of elements. This process nucleates nanoscopic SRO regions which act as local stress concentrators, thereby reducing toughness and promoting brittle fracture in areas subject to high deformation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undisturbed (baseline) alloy, loaded specimens will show emergence of nanoscale chemically ordered clusters at deformation sites correlating with crack initiation zones, along with an observable reduction in overall toughness. This behavior is distinct from conventional alloys, where embrittlement is typically associated with grain-boundary precipitation.
drafts.baseline: The alloy in its as-processed, single-phase, homogeneously disordered state without significant local compositional fluctuations or SRO.
drafts.boundary: The effect is expected to become significant under service conditions involving high cumulative strain at temperatures where diffusion is sufficiently activated; under very low temperatures or minimal deformation, the mechanism may not be operative due to limited atomic mobility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the same single-phase HEA and subject them to a range of controlled cyclic deformation experiments under identical temperature conditions. Use high-resolution in situ characterization techniques (such as TEM with EDS or atom probe tomography) to map the evolution of local chemical order and monitor sites of crack initiation. A parallel set of conventional alloy samples known to embrittle via grain-boundary processes should be tested under the same conditions as a controlled comparison.
measurements: High-resolution imaging (TEM, APT) to detect nanoscale compositional fluctuations and SRO regions
Correlation analysis between localized SRO formation and crack initiation points
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If in the deformed HEA samples there is no measurable formation of localized SRO or compositional heterogeneity (i.e., the alloy maintains its homogeneous disordered state) and toughness remains unchanged relative to the baseline despite high strain, then the proposed mechanism is falsified. Similarly, if crack initiation sites do not correlate with any detectable compositional redistribution, the hypothesis would be invalidated.
